q2: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(TIME_SLOT_ID)>5) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ only in their HAVING clause thresholds: Q1 counts TIME_SLOT_ID > 4, while Q2 counts TIME_SLOT_ID > 5. This means Q1 will include students who have exactly 5 courses in the same time slot and year, while Q2 will exclude them.
counterexample: INSERT INTO STUDENT (ID, NAME, DEPT_NAME, TOT_CRED) VALUES (1, 'Alice', 'CS', 100); INSERT INTO SECTION (COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, BUILDING, ROOM_NUMBER, TIME_SLOT_ID) VALUES (101, 1, 2023, 'A', 101, 'TS1'), (102, 1, 2023, 'A', 102, 'TS1'), (103, 1, 2023, 'A', 103, 'TS1'), (104, 1, 2023, 'A', 104, 'TS1'), (105, 1, 2023, 'A', 105, 'TS1'); INSERT INTO TAKES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, GRADE) VALUES (1, 101, 1, 2023, 'A'), (1, 102, 1, 2023, 'B'), (1, 103, 1, 2023, 'C'), (1, 104, 1, 2023, 'B'), (1, 105, 1, 2023, 'A');
counterexample_dsp: Create a student who takes exactly 5 courses in the same time slot and year. Q1 will include this student (since 5 > 4), but Q2 will exclude them (since 5 is not > 5).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE) AS A ON COURSE.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
q2: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE GROUP BY DEPT_NAME) AS A ON COURSE.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
explanation: Q1 finds departments that offer courses with the maximum credits across all departments, while Q2 finds departments that offer courses with the maximum credits within each department. Q2 may return departments that don't have the global maximum credits but have the highest credits within their own department.
counterexample: INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (1, 101, 'CS', 3); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (2, 102, 'CS', 4); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (3, 201, 'Math', 2); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (4, 202, 'Math', 3);
counterexample_dsp: Create two departments: 'CS' with courses having 3 and 4 credits, and 'Math' with courses having 2 and 3 credits. The global maximum credit is 4 (only in CS), but Q2 will also return 'Math' because it has a course with 3 credits, which is the maximum within the Math department.

q1: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.YEAR, F.MONTH_ID, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
q2: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(C.CID) > 1000
explanation: Q1 groups by C.NAME, F.YEAR, F.MONTH_ID, F.DAY_OF_MONTH and counts F.FID, while Q2 groups by C.NAME, F.DAY_OF_MONTH and counts C.CID. The difference arises because Q1's grouping is finer (includes year and month_id) and counts flight IDs, while Q2's grouping is coarser (only day_of_month) and counts carrier IDs, which can lead to different counts and different HAVING filter results.
counterexample: INSERT INTO CARRIERS (CID, NAME) VALUES (1, 100); INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID) VALUES (1, 2023, 1, 15, 1), (2, 2024, 1, 15, 1), (3, 2023, 2, 15, 1);
counterexample_dsp: Create a carrier with multiple flights on the same day_of_month but across different years or months. This makes Q1's groups (per day, month, year) each have <= 1000 flights, but Q2's group (per day across all months/years) has > 1000 carrier counts, causing Q2 to return the carrier name while Q1 returns nothing.

q1: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.CID, C.NAME, F.YEAR, F.MONTH_ID, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
q2: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
explanation: Q1 groups by C.CID, C.NAME, F.YEAR, F.MONTH_ID, F.DAY_OF_MONTH while Q2 groups by C.NAME, F.DAY_OF_MONTH only. This means Q1 counts flights per carrier per day per month per year, while Q2 counts flights per carrier name per day across all months and years. If a carrier has the same name but different CID values, or if flights on the same day of month but different months/years exceed 1000 in Q2 but not in Q1, the results will differ.
counterexample: INSERT INTO CARRIERS (CID, NAME) VALUES (1, 100), (2, 100); INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID) VALUES (1, 2023, 1, 15, 1), (2, 2023, 1, 15, 1), (3, 2023, 2, 15, 1), (4, 2023, 2, 15, 1), (5, 2023, 1, 15, 2), (6, 2023, 1, 15, 2), (7, 2023, 2, 15, 2), (8, 2023, 2, 15, 2); INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID) SELECT FID + 8, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID FROM FLIGHTS; INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID) SELECT FID + 16, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID FROM FLIGHTS; INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID) SELECT FID + 32, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID FROM FLIGHTS; INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID) SELECT FID + 64, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID FROM FLIGHTS; INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID) SELECT FID + 128, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID FROM FLIGHTS; INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID) SELECT FID + 256, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID FROM FLIGHTS; INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID) SELECT FID + 512, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID FROM FLIGHTS;
counterexample_dsp: Two carriers with the same NAME but different CID values have flights on the same DAY_OF_MONTH but different MONTH_ID/YEAR combinations. In Q1, each carrier-day-month-year group has ≤1000 flights, so no results. In Q2, the grouping by NAME and DAY_OF_MONTH combines flights from both carriers and different months/years, exceeding 1000 flights.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT F.ORIGIN_CITY, F.DEST_CITY, F.ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F JOIN (SELECT A.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(A.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS A GROUP BY A.ORIGIN_CITY) AS X ON F.ORIGIN_CITY = X.ORIGIN_CITY AND F.ACTUAL_TIME = X.MAX_TIME
q2: SELECT S.ORIGIN_CITY, F2.DEST_CITY, MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) FROM (SELECT F1.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(F1.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F1 GROUP BY F1.ORIGIN_CITY) AS S JOIN FLIGHTS AS F2 ON S.ORIGIN_CITY = F2.ORIGIN_CITY AND F2.ACTUAL_TIME = S.MAX_TIME GROUP BY S.ORIGIN_CITY, F2.DEST_CITY
explanation: Q1 finds all flights with the maximum actual_time for each origin_city, while Q2 groups by both origin_city and dest_city after finding the maximum actual_time per origin_city. The key difference is that Q2 can return multiple rows per origin_city if there are multiple destinations with the same maximum actual_time, whereas Q1 returns one row per origin_city regardless of destination.
counterexample: INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, ORIGIN_CITY, DEST_CITY, ACTUAL_TIME) VALUES (1, 1, 2, 100); INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, ORIGIN_CITY, DEST_CITY, ACTUAL_TIME) VALUES (2, 1, 3, 100); INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, ORIGIN_CITY, DEST_CITY, ACTUAL_TIME) VALUES (3, 2, 4, 200);
counterexample_dsp: Create test data where one origin city has multiple destinations with the same maximum actual_time value. Q1 will return one row per origin city, while Q2 will return multiple rows for that origin city (one per destination with the maximum time).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT F.ORIGIN_CITY, F.DEST_CITY, F.ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F JOIN (SELECT A.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(A.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS A GROUP BY A.ORIGIN_CITY) AS X ON F.ORIGIN_CITY = X.ORIGIN_CITY AND F.ACTUAL_TIME = X.MAX_TIME
q2: SELECT P.ORIGIN_CITY, P.DEST_CITY, P.ACTUAL_TIME FROM (SELECT F1.ORIGIN_CITY, F1.DEST_CITY, F1.ACTUAL_TIME, MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F1 JOIN FLIGHTS AS F2 ON F1.ORIGIN_CITY = F2.ORIGIN_CITY GROUP BY F1.ORIGIN_CITY, F1.DEST_CITY, F1.ACTUAL_TIME) AS P WHERE P.ACTUAL_TIME = P.MAX_ACTUAL_TIME
explanation: Q1 finds flights with maximum actual_time per origin_city. Q2 incorrectly groups by origin_city, dest_city, and actual_time, then compares each flight's actual_time against the maximum actual_time across all flights from that origin_city. This can cause Q2 to return duplicate origin_city entries when multiple flights from the same origin_city have the same maximum actual_time but different dest_cities, while Q1 returns only one flight per origin_city.
counterexample: INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, ORIGIN_CITY, DEST_CITY, ACTUAL_TIME) VALUES (1, 1, 2, 100); INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, ORIGIN_CITY, DEST_CITY, ACTUAL_TIME) VALUES (2, 1, 3, 100);
counterexample_dsp: Two flights from the same origin_city with the same maximum actual_time but different dest_cities. Q1 returns one flight (arbitrary choice), Q2 returns both flights.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS)>10 AND COUNT(C.CREDITS)>5
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS)>10 AND COUNT(C.CREDITS)>8
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in their HAVING clause conditions: Q1 requires COUNT(C.CREDITS)>5 while Q2 requires COUNT(C.CREDITS)>8. This means Q1 will include departments with 6-8 courses having total credits > 10, while Q2 will exclude them.
counterexample: INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT (DEPT_NAME, BUILDING, BUDGET) VALUES (1, 1, 100000); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (1, 1, 1, 2), (2, 2, 1, 2), (3, 3, 1, 2), (4, 4, 1, 2), (5, 5, 1, 2), (6, 6, 1, 2), (7, 7, 1, 2);
counterexample_dsp: Create a department with exactly 7 courses where the total credits sum to >10. Q1 will include this department (7 > 5) while Q2 will exclude it (7 ≤ 8).

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY)>100 AND MAX(I.SALARY)<75
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY)>=100 AND MAX(I.SALARY)<75
explanation: Q1 uses SUM(I.SALARY)>100 while Q2 uses SUM(I.SALARY)>=100 in the HAVING clause. The difference occurs when the sum of salaries exactly equals 100 - Q1 will exclude such groups while Q2 will include them.
counterexample: INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT (DEPT_NAME, BUILDING, BUDGET) VALUES (1, 1, 1000); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (1, 1, 1, 3); INSERT INTO INSTRUCTOR (ID, NAME, SALARY, DEPT_NAME) VALUES (1, 1, 50, 1); INSERT INTO INSTRUCTOR (ID, NAME, SALARY, DEPT_NAME) VALUES (2, 2, 50, 1);
counterexample_dsp: Create a department with exactly 2 instructors where the sum of their salaries equals 100 and both salaries are below 75. Q1 will exclude this department while Q2 will include it.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET)>100000 AND COUNT(D.BUDGET)>10
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET)>100000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET)>10
explanation: Q1 uses COUNT(D.BUDGET) which counts all budget values (including duplicates), while Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET) which counts only unique budget values. They differ when there are duplicate budget values within the same department.
counterexample_dsp: Create a scenario where one department has more than 10 courses with the same budget value (so COUNT(D.BUDGET) > 10 but COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET) = 1), and the sum of budgets exceeds 100000.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)>4
explanation: Q1 requires exactly 4 distinct salary values in each department group (COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4), while Q2 requires more than 4 distinct salary values (COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)>4). A department with exactly 4 distinct salaries will appear in Q1 but not in Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Create a department 'Math' with exactly 4 distinct instructor salaries (50000, 60000, 70000, 80000) and average salary > 50000. This department will appear in Q1 (exactly 4 distinct salaries) but not in Q2 (not more than 4 distinct salaries).

q1: SELECT T.SEMESTER, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM DEPARTMENT D INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4) INNER JOIN COURSE C ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY T.SEMESTER HAVING AVG(C.CREDITS)>2 AND COUNT(D.BUILDING)=2
q2: SELECT T.SEMESTER, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM DEPARTMENT D INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4) INNER JOIN COURSE C ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY T.SEMESTER HAVING AVG(C.CREDITS)>2 AND COUNT(D.BUILDING)>=2
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in their HAVING clause conditions: Q1 requires COUNT(D.BUILDING)=2 (exactly 2 buildings), while Q2 requires COUNT(D.BUILDING)>=2 (2 or more buildings). This means Q1 will exclude groups with more than 2 buildings, while Q2 will include them.
counterexample: INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT (DEPT_NAME, BUILDING, BUDGET) VALUES (1, 1, 2020), (1, 2, 2020), (1, 3, 2020); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (1, 1, 1, 3), (2, 2, 1, 3); INSERT INTO TEACHES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, SEMESTER, INSTRUCTOR) VALUES (1, 1, 1, 2016, 1, 1), (1, 2, 1, 2016, 1, 1);
counterexample_dsp: Create data where for a specific semester, there are 3 different buildings in the joined DEPARTMENT records, with average credits > 2. Q1 will exclude this semester (COUNT=3 ≠ 2), while Q2 will include it (COUNT=3 ≥ 2).

q1: SELECT ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID,DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
q2: SELECT ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
explanation: Q1 groups by both ID and DEPT_NAME, counting the number of courses per student per department. Q2 groups only by ID, counting all courses across departments for each student. The difference occurs when a student takes courses from multiple departments: Q1 requires at least 2 courses in the same department, while Q2 requires at least 2 courses total across departments.
counterexample: INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT (DEPT_NAME, BUILDING, BUDGET) VALUES (1, 1, 1000), (2, 2, 2000); INSERT INTO STUDENT (ID, NAME, DEPT_NAME, TOT_CRED) VALUES (1, 1, 1, 0); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (1, 1, 1, 3), (2, 2, 2, 3); INSERT INTO SECTION (COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, BUILDING, ROOM_NUMBER, TIME_SLOT_ID) VALUES (1, 1, 2023, 1, 101, 1), (2, 1, 2023, 2, 201, 2); INSERT INTO TAKES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, GRADE) VALUES (1, 1, 1, 2023, 4), (1, 2, 1, 2023, 4);
counterexample_dsp: A student takes one course from department A and one course from department B. Q1 returns empty (no department with ≥2 courses), Q2 returns the student (total courses ≥2).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(COURSE_ID)>2)
q2: SELECT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(COURSE_ID)>2)
explanation: Q1 uses DISTINCT while Q2 does not. If multiple courses from the same department have the maximum credits that satisfy the subquery condition, Q2 will return duplicate department names while Q1 will return only unique ones.
counterexample: INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT (DEPT_NAME, BUILDING, BUDGET) VALUES (1, 100, 50000); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (101, 1, 1, 4); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (102, 1, 1, 4); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (103, 1, 1, 4); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (104, 1, 1, 4);
counterexample_dsp: Create a CS department with multiple courses having the same maximum credits value that satisfies the subquery condition (more than 2 courses in the department). This will cause Q2 to return duplicate department names while Q1 returns only unique ones.

q1: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING COUNT(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
q2: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING SUM(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in their HAVING clauses within the subquery. Q1 uses COUNT(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1, which checks if a student has multiple sections with the same TIME_SLOT_ID and YEAR. Q2 uses SUM(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1, which sums the TIME_SLOT_ID values (numeric IDs) and checks if the sum exceeds 1. This means Q1 identifies students with time slot conflicts (same time slot/year), while Q2 identifies students where the sum of time slot IDs exceeds 1, which can occur even without conflicts.
counterexample: INSERT INTO STUDENT (ID, NAME, DEPT_NAME, TOT_CRED) VALUES (1, 'Alice', 1, 30); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (101, 1, 1, 3), (102, 2, 1, 3); INSERT INTO SECTION (COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, BUILDING, ROOM_NUMBER, TIME_SLOT_ID) VALUES (101, 1, 2023, 1, 101, 1), (102, 1, 2024, 1, 102, 1); INSERT INTO TAKES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, GRADE) VALUES (1, 101, 1, 2023, 85), (1, 102, 1, 2024, 90);
counterexample_dsp: The test data includes a student who takes two sections in different years (avoiding time slot conflicts for Q1) but with TIME_SLOT_ID values that sum to more than 1 (satisfying Q2). This makes the student appear in Q2's result but not in Q1's.

q1: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR, COURSE_ID HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
q2: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
explanation: Q1 groups by both YEAR and COURSE_ID before filtering with HAVING COUNT(ID)>4, meaning it counts instructors per course per year. Q2 groups only by YEAR before filtering, counting all instructors per year regardless of course. The difference occurs when multiple courses in the same year each have >4 instructors, but the total instructors per year is not >4.
counterexample: INSERT INTO INSTRUCTOR (ID, NAME, SALARY, DEPT_NAME) VALUES (1, 'A', 50000, 'CS'), (2, 'B', 60000, 'CS'), (3, 'C', 55000, 'CS'), (4, 'D', 52000, 'CS'), (5, 'E', 58000, 'CS'), (6, 'F', 53000, 'CS'); INSERT INTO TEACHES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, SEMESTER, INSTRUCTOR) VALUES (1, 'C1', 1, 2023, 'Fall', 1), (2, 'C1', 1, 2023, 'Fall', 2), (3, 'C1', 1, 2023, 'Fall', 3), (4, 'C2', 1, 2023, 'Fall', 4), (5, 'C2', 1, 2023, 'Fall', 5), (6, 'C2', 1, 2023, 'Fall', 6);
counterexample_dsp: In year 2023, two courses (C1 and C2) each have 3 instructors, so no course has >4 instructors. But combined, year 2023 has 6 instructors total. Q1 returns no rows (no course meets >4 instructors), Q2 returns 2023 (year total >4 instructors).

q1: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE
q2: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS > 3
explanation: Q1 returns all courses regardless of their credit value, while Q2 only returns courses with CREDITS > 3. Therefore, any course with CREDITS ≤ 3 will appear in Q1 but not in Q2.
counterexample: INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (1, 101, 1, 3); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (2, 102, 1, 4);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one course with CREDITS = 3 (which Q1 includes but Q2 excludes) and one course with CREDITS = 4 (which both queries include).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID = TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
q2: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID >= TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
explanation: Q1 uses an equality join (COURSE.COURSE_ID = TEACHES.COURSE_ID) while Q2 uses a range comparison (COURSE.COURSE_ID >= TEACHES.COURSE_ID). This means Q2 will match courses with IDs greater than or equal to the taught course IDs, potentially creating many-to-many matches that don't exist in Q1.
